passage:
Mohit threw his spoon and screamed. "No! No!"
"Mohit, stop that," Ayesha said. "Eat your khichdi nicely."
He shoved the bowl away and grabbed at her plate.
"Hey! That's rude."
Dadi looked up from the stove. "Ayesha, when did he last eat?"
Ayesha glanced at the clock. "Breakfast. The market took forever."
"He's hungry, not naughty."
Ayesha cooled a spoonful and held it out. Mohit gulped it, then another. His sobs slowed to hiccups.

qa.q: Why had Mohit gone so long without eating?
qa.a: The market took forever.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he grabbed at Ayesha's plate?
qa.a: He was hungry and distressed, and grabbing and screaming were the only ways he could show it.

qa.q: What worked better than scolding, and why?
qa.a: Feeding him a cooled spoonful right away; a hungry toddler calms once food arrives, not after a telling-off.

qa.q: How does Ayesha read the screaming at first?
qa.a: She reads it as rudeness and scolds him, until Dadi's question makes her see he is hungry.

grounding: Shows a hungry toddler who cannot say so screaming, throwing and grabbing, and food ending the outburst faster than discipline.

passage: Creche note for Pema's family, Friday. Pema arrived late and missed our morning snack. By late morning she was snatching other children's biscuits, throwing her cup and refusing even the banana she loves. She couldn't tell us why. The book showed nothing since an early breakfast. I sat her down with fruit and rice; she ate in silence and was soon building towers again. On late days we will feed her as soon as she arrives. Vijay (creche teacher)

qa.q: What did Pema refuse even though she usually loves it?
qa.a: The banana.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she threw her cup?
qa.a: She was hungry and upset but could not say so, so the distress came out as snatching and throwing.

qa.q: What plan did Vijay make, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: To give Pema something to eat as soon as she arrives on late days; keeping food regular can stop the tantrum before it starts.

qa.q: How might the other children have been affected?
qa.a: They had biscuits snatched from them and may have felt upset or confused, not knowing Pema was just hungry.

grounding: Illustrates a hungry toddler showing need through grabbing, throwing and refusing food, and regular feeding settling her.

passage: The local bus to Karad was an hour late, and lunch was still in the tiffin. Little Bhupen began to wail, grabbing at a stranger's banana, then pushing away the water Keerthana offered. He threw his cap on the floor. "Hungry, na?" she said, opening the tiffin on her lap. She tore off a soft piece of chapati. He grabbed it with both hands. Two mouthfuls later he was quiet, leaning on her arm, watching the fields.

qa.q: What did Bhupen grab at?
qa.a: A stranger's banana.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when he threw his cap?
qa.a: He was hungry and cross, and too little to say so, so it came out as wailing and throwing.

qa.q: What ended the crying?
qa.a: Keerthana fed him soft chapati from the tiffin instead of scolding, which met his real need.

qa.q: How might the stranger with the banana see Bhupen?
qa.a: The stranger might think he was just naughty, not a hungry toddler whose lunch was late.

grounding: Shows a hungry toddler who cannot say so crying, grabbing and throwing, and food ending it faster than discipline.

passage: At the park in Lisbon, Noa refused the swing, refused the slide, then threw the sand bucket at Priscila's feet and howled. Priscila checked her watch: nearly one, and breakfast had been early. She sat Noa on the bench and pulled out rice crackers and a little box of cut pear. A small hand shot out. Within a few bites the howling became hiccups, then a sticky grin. Priscila typed a note on her phone: snack at eleven, every park day.

qa.q: What time was it when Priscila checked her watch?
qa.a: Nearly one.

qa.q: What does Noa's refusing everything and throwing the bucket suggest?
qa.a: Noa was hungry and frustrated but could not say it, so the upset came out as refusing and throwing.

qa.q: What lesson did Priscila take for next time?
qa.a: To give a snack at eleven on park days, keeping a regular rhythm so hunger does not turn into a tantrum.

qa.q: How might Priscila have felt when the bucket landed at her feet?
qa.a: She may have felt startled and irritated at first, but calm enough to check the time and think of food.

grounding: Shows a hungry toddler refusing everything and throwing things, and a regular snack rhythm ending it better than discipline.

passage:
Monday: Lunch was late because of guests. By two, Samir threw his rice bowl to the floor and screamed when Zeenat picked it up.
Wednesday: Zeenat kept lunch at twelve-thirty, guests or not. Samir ate, sang to his spoon, and fell asleep.
Friday: Shopping ran long. At the first whine, Zeenat gave him a banana from her bag. He munched it in the trolley, pointing at the oranges.

qa.q: What did Samir throw on Monday?
qa.a: His rice bowl.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he screamed on Monday?
qa.a: He was hungry and upset, and with lunch late he had no words for it, only screaming and throwing.

qa.q: What did Zeenat change, and why did it work?
qa.a: She kept lunch at a regular time and carried a snack, so hunger was met before it became a tantrum.

qa.q: What is Monday like for Zeenat?
qa.a: She is juggling guests and a screaming toddler, likely frazzled until she sees the late lunch was the cause.

grounding: Shows a toddler's hunger coming out as throwing and screaming, and a regular feeding rhythm preventing the tantrums.

passage: The plumber came at noon, and lunch in the Chennai flat slid to half past one. Akash pushed away the banana Payal offered, then howled and threw his spoon. When she put rice on his tray, he swept it to the floor. 'Stop that!' she began, then looked at the clock. His lunch was over an hour late. She sat beside him, took a small spoonful of soft dal-rice and blew on it. Akash opened his mouth. Five spoons later he was smiling and banging the tray.

qa.q: What time did lunch slide to?
qa.a: Half past one.

qa.q: Why did Akash throw the spoon and sweep the rice away?
qa.a: He was hungry and miserable but couldn't say so, so his distress came out as crying and throwing.

qa.q: What worked better than 'Stop that!'?
qa.a: Payal noticed lunch was late and calmly fed him small spoonfuls, which ended the tantrum.

qa.q: What might Payal have felt when she looked at the clock?
qa.a: Payal likely felt a pang of guilt, realising Akash's meal was over an hour late.

grounding: A hungry toddler shows it by crying and throwing food, and feeding him ends the tantrum faster than discipline.
